title: The Recall-to-Output Gap: When a Model Knows a Fact but States Its Opposite

original_idea.quick_reasoning: Clearly addresses an AI Safety problem with a reasonably scoped approach.

theory_of_impact.reasoning: Plausible with gap: understanding whether the recall-to-output gap is a routing failure or MLP suppression determines intervention strategy, but the chain from mechanistic understanding to deployed safety improvement is indirect for hallucination-under-pressure.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: Building misleading-context datasets and probing the residual stream via TransformerLens at the final token position is intermediate. Causal patching to restore correct-answer features is well-documented in tutorials.

narrow_scope.reasoning: Focused deliverable: build dataset, probe for correct-answer feature presence across layers, identify where displacement happens (routing vs suppression), and measure accuracy recovery via patching. Clear experimental arc.

novelty.reasoning: Research has established that models 'know what they don't know' — internal activations differ when guessing vs recalling. Work on sycophancy shows LLM activations encapsulate internal beliefs that can diverge from generated outputs (ICLR 2026). Linear directions encoding self-knowledge have been found causally relevant for refusal behavior. Mechanistic Interpretability for hallucination has advanced (ICLR 2026 paper on mechanistic interpretability). However, the specific framing of a 'recall-to-output gap' — where a model internally recalls a correct fact but outputs the opposite under misleading context — and the mechanistic question of whether this is a routing failure vs MLP suppression has not been directly studied in this precise formulation.
